title: Jewish, Christian and Academic Readings of the Same Text
bigQuestion: When a rabbi, a pastor and a historian open the same chapter, what is each of them asking, and how can we describe their readings without ranking them?

story.title: Three Readers, One Chapter
story.kicker: In a Chicago classroom, three guests read Isaiah 53 aloud and reach three different places.
paragraphs: The seniors in Ms. Okafor's world religions class have three guests. One is a rabbi from a congregation in Lakeview. One is a pastor from a church on the South Side. One is a professor of ancient history from a university downtown. Ms. Okafor has asked each to read Isaiah 53 and say what it is about. She has told the students the rule for the hour: describe, do not rank.

The rabbi reads first, from the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation. She stops at the word "servant." Isaiah, she says, has already named the servant several times, and in chapter 41 and chapter 49 the servant is Israel. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all read chapter 53 that way: a people despised by the nations and then vindicated. She adds that the Talmud, in one passage, reads a verse of this chapter about the Messiah, so Jewish tradition is not of one voice either.

The pastor reads the same chapter from the King James Version. He stops at the line about a man bearing the griefs of others. For Christians, he says, this is one of the clearest pictures of Jesus in the Hebrew Bible. He points to the book of Acts, where an Ethiopian official is reading this very chapter and asks whom the prophet means. The early church answered: Jesus. He is careful to say that this is how his tradition reads it.

The professor reads last, from a scholarly translation. She asks a different question. Who wrote these chapters, and when? Most historians, she says, place Isaiah 40 through 55 in the Babylonian exile, around 540 BCE, well after the Isaiah of Jerusalem. The servant, on that reading, is a figure the exiles could recognize, perhaps the community itself, perhaps the prophet. She is not saying who the servant is. She is saying what the text's first hearers could have heard.

A student raises a hand. "So who is right?" Ms. Okafor lets the silence sit. Then the professor says, "We are not asking the same question." The rabbi and the pastor nod. This chapter is about that sentence. It looks at the same texts, Isaiah 7, Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and Genesis 1, through Jewish, Christian and academic eyes. It visits a courtroom in Paris and a palace in Barcelona where the reading of texts was forced into a contest. And it ends with the readers of the last two centuries, who asked new questions of their own.
story.think: The professor says the three readers are not asking the same question. What is each one's question, and how would you know if one of them had answered it well?

lessons.title: Tanakh and Old Testament
lessons.mainIdea: The Jewish Tanakh and the Christian Old Testament contain the same core books but count, order and sometimes translate them differently, and the difference shapes what each reader sees.
reading: A *canon* is the list of books a community counts as scripture. The Jewish canon is the *Tanakh*, twenty-four books in three parts: Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim. Christians call roughly the same collection the *Old Testament*, a name that pairs it with a New Testament. Jewish readers do not use "Old Testament" for their own scripture, since for them it is not old in relation to anything. In a public school, the neutral name is Hebrew Bible.

The counts differ because of how books are grouped. The Tanakh counts Samuel, Kings, Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah as one book each and the twelve minor prophets as one book, the Twelve. Protestant Bibles split them, which gives thirty-nine books with the same content. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles add books such as Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom and Sirach, giving forty-six or more. Jewish tradition and Protestants call these apocrypha; Catholics call them deuterocanonical.

Translation adds another layer. The *Septuagint*, a Greek translation made by Jews in Egypt from about the third century BCE, became the Bible of the early church. It includes the extra books and sometimes reads a verse differently from the Hebrew. Jerome's Latin *Vulgate*, finished around 405 CE, went back to the Hebrew for most books. When a rabbi and a pastor read "the same verse," they may be reading different words.

None of this makes one canon right and another wrong. It means that when you compare readings, you first ask which canon, which order and which translation each reader holds. That is a matter of fact, not of faith, and it is where careful comparison begins.

words.d: the list of books a religious community counts as its scripture
the Jewish Bible of 24 books in three parts: Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings)
the Christian name for the Hebrew scriptures, paired with the New Testament; counts and order vary by church
the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures made by Jews in Egypt from about the 3rd century BCE
Jerome's Latin translation of the Bible, finished c. 405 CE, long the standard Bible of the Western church

look.title: Counting the Same Books
look.cite: Standard counts; the Tanakh's 24 count Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra–Nehemiah and the Twelve as one book each; Orthodox counts vary by church
look.prompt: The Tanakh and the Protestant Old Testament have the same content. Why are the numbers 24 and 39, and what does the Catholic count add?

check.q: Why does the Tanakh count 24 books while a Protestant Old Testament counts 39 with the same content?
choices: The Tanakh leaves out the Prophets
The Tanakh groups Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra–Nehemiah and the Twelve as single books
check.why: The content is the same; the Tanakh counts several paired or grouped books as one each.

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: A Greek translation made by Jews in Egypt from about the 3rd century BCE
check.why: The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation that became the Bible of the early church.

check.q: Which books does a Catholic Old Testament include that the Tanakh does not?
check.why: Catholic Bibles include deuterocanonical books such as Tobit, Judith and 1 and 2 Maccabees.

lessons.title: Order Matters
lessons.mainIdea: The Tanakh ends with Chronicles and a call to go up to Jerusalem, while the Christian Old Testament ends with Malachi and the promise of Elijah, and each ending prepares a different next chapter.
reading: The books are the same, but the order is not. The Tanakh puts the Prophets in the middle and the Writings last. The *Ketuvim*, the Writings, close with Ezra–Nehemiah and then *Chronicles*. The last verses of 2 Chronicles record the decree of Cyrus, king of Persia, allowing the exiles to return and rebuild the Temple. The last word is a call to go up. Jewish readers have long noted that their Bible ends on the way home.

The Christian Old Testament follows the Septuagint's order. It moves history to the front, the poetry to the middle and the Prophets to the end. Its final book is *Malachi*, whose last verses promise that Elijah the prophet will come before the great day of the LORD. In a Christian Bible the next page is the Gospel of Matthew, where John the Baptist appears in the wilderness. Christian readers have seen the ending as a bridge to that story.

Neither community moved a book to make a point in secret. The orders grew up over centuries and both are ancient. But once fixed, an order teaches. A Jewish student who reads through the Tanakh finishes with return and rebuilding. A Christian student finishes with expectation. The historian notes both orders and asks when each became standard, which is a question about manuscripts and lists, not about truth.

The lesson for comparison is simple. Before you ask what a book means, ask where it sits. The same chapter of Daniel is among the Prophets in a Christian Bible and among the Writings in the Tanakh. That placement already tells you how each reader has been taught to hear it.

words.d: the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh, which ends with Chronicles
the last book of the Tanakh; it ends with Cyrus's decree allowing the exiles to return
the last of the Twelve prophets and the last book of the Christian Old Testament
the Prophets, the second part of the Tanakh, which the Christian order moves to the end

look.title: The Last Verse of the Tanakh
look.text: The final verse of 2 Chronicles gives the words of Cyrus, king of Persia: the LORD, the God of heaven, has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build a house in Jerusalem, and whoever among the people belongs to the LORD, may God be with him, and let him go up.
look.cite: 2 Chronicles 36:23, paraphrased from the Jewish Publication Society translation (1917)
look.prompt: Compare this ending with Malachi's promise of Elijah. What mood does each leave a reader in, and what does each invite the reader to do next?

check.q: Which book closes the Tanakh?
check.why: The Ketuvim, and so the Tanakh, end with Chronicles and Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem.

check.q: Which book closes the Christian Old Testament?
check.why: The Christian order places the Prophets last, ending with Malachi and the promise of Elijah.

check.q: Where is the book of Daniel placed in the Tanakh?
check.why: The Tanakh puts Daniel in the Ketuvim; Christian Bibles place it with the Prophets.

lessons.title: Isaiah 7:14 in Two Translations
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah 7:14 shows how one Hebrew word, almah, became a dividing line, with Jewish translators reading "young woman," the Greek Septuagint and Christian tradition reading "virgin," and historians asking about King Ahaz.
reading: In Isaiah 7 the prophet speaks to *Ahaz*, king of Judah, around 734 BCE, when two neighboring kings threaten Jerusalem. Isaiah offers a sign: a young woman will bear a son and name him *Immanuel*, "God is with us," and before the child is old enough to know right from wrong, the threat will pass. The Hebrew word for the woman is *almah*. In the Tanakh it means a young woman of marriageable age. It does not by itself say whether she is married.

The Septuagint translated almah with the Greek word parthenos, which usually means virgin. The Gospel of Matthew (1:23) quotes that Greek line and applies it to the birth of Jesus. From then on, Christian readers, from the church fathers to the King James Version, read Isaiah 7:14 as a prophecy of a virgin birth. That reading is central to Christian tradition and is stated here as its reading.

Jewish commentators read the verse within its chapter. Rashi takes the young woman to be the prophet's own wife, and the sign to be for Ahaz in his own lifetime. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it similarly and point out that a sign for Ahaz must come in Ahaz's day. Radak adds that the Hebrew word for virgin is a different word, betulah. The 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders the phrase "the young woman." So does the Christian Revised Standard Version of 1952, which caused a public dispute in American churches.

The historian's question is narrower. What did the sign mean to Ahaz? Most scholars connect the child to the crisis of 734 BCE and to the chapters that follow, where Isaiah's own son is named as a sign. On that reading, the verse is about Judah's survival, and its later use in Matthew is a second life the text took on. That is a description of how readings grow, not a ruling on which one a reader should hold.

words.d: the Hebrew word in Isaiah 7:14 for a young woman of marriageable age; translated "young woman" by JPS 1917 and "virgin" by the Septuagint and KJV
king of Judah, c. 734 BCE, to whom Isaiah offered the sign in Isaiah 7
the child's name in Isaiah 7:14; it means "God is with us"
the Greek word the Septuagint used for almah; it usually means virgin

look.title: A Sign for Ahaz
look.text: Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
look.cite: Isaiah 7:14, King James Version (1611); the Jewish Publication Society translation (1917) reads "the young woman"
look.prompt: Read the verse once as a sign given to King Ahaz about the next few years and once as Matthew 1:23 reads it. What does each reader have to assume about the word almah and about the timing of the sign?

check.q: How does the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation render almah in Isaiah 7:14?
check.why: JPS 1917 reads "the young woman"; the KJV, following the Septuagint's parthenos, reads "a virgin."

check.q: To whom does Isaiah offer the sign in Isaiah 7?
check.why: Isaiah addresses Ahaz, king of Judah, during the crisis of c. 734 BCE.

check.q: Which Gospel quotes the Septuagint's version of Isaiah 7:14?
check.why: Matthew 1:23 quotes the Greek line and applies it to the birth of Jesus.

lessons.title: Isaiah 53: Who Is the Servant?
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish commentators mostly read the servant of Isaiah 53 as Israel, Christian tradition reads him as Jesus, and historians ask what the exiles heard; each reading answers a different question.
reading: Isaiah 52:13 through 53:12 describes a *servant* who is despised, suffers for others and is finally raised up. Scholars call it the fourth of the *servant songs* in Isaiah 40 through 55. Earlier in those chapters the servant is named: in Isaiah 41:8 and 49:3 the servant is Israel, or Jacob. The identity of the servant in chapter 53 is the most argued question in the whole book.

Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak read the servant as the people of Israel, humiliated among the nations in exile and then vindicated. On this reading, the speakers who say "he was despised" are the nations themselves, astonished at Israel's rise. The church father Origen, writing around 248 CE, reports that Jewish scholars of his day already read the chapter this way. Jewish tradition is not uniform, though. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b) applies a verse of the chapter to the Messiah, and some later Jewish readers followed that line.

Christian tradition, from the New Testament on, reads the servant as Jesus. The book of Acts (8:26–35) tells of an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah 53 and asking whether the prophet speaks of himself or another, and the apostle Philip answers with the story of Jesus. Church fathers and later Christian readers built on this. In Christian worship the chapter is read in Holy Week. Jewish readers note that it is not among the haftarot read in the synagogue year, which some take as deliberate and others as chance.

Historians place Isaiah 40 through 55 in Babylon around 540 BCE, near the fall of that empire to Cyrus. They ask what the exiles could have heard: perhaps the community, perhaps the prophet, perhaps a figure the text leaves open on purpose. Literary readers point to the shifting speakers and the poem's refusal to name the servant. Three readers, three questions. A good comparison names each question before comparing any answer.

words.d: four poems in Isaiah 40–55 about a servant of the LORD; Isaiah 52:13–53:12 is the fourth
the figure of Isaiah 53, read by most Jewish commentators as Israel and by Christian tradition as Jesus
a Christian scholar of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253 CE) who reported that Jewish readers took Isaiah 53 as about the people
the reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah reading in the synagogue; Isaiah 53 is not among them

look.title: He Hath Borne Our Griefs
look.text: Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
look.prompt: Who is "we" in this verse? Try the verse with "we" as the nations speaking about Israel, as Rashi reads it, and with "we" as Christians speaking about Jesus. What changes, and what stays the same?

check.q: How do Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak read the servant of Isaiah 53?
check.why: The major medieval Jewish commentators read the servant as Israel, despised in exile and then vindicated.

check.q: Which New Testament book tells of an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah 53?
check.why: Acts 8:26–35 has Philip explain the chapter to the Ethiopian official as being about Jesus.

check.q: Which Jewish text applies a verse of Isaiah 53 to the Messiah, showing Jewish tradition is not of one voice?
check.why: The Talmud in Sanhedrin 98b reads a verse of Isaiah 53 about the Messiah, while the medieval commentators read Israel.

lessons.title: Psalm 22: A Cry in Two Traditions
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 22 is read in Jewish tradition as David's prayer and, in the midrash, as Esther's, and in Christian tradition as the words of Jesus on the cross; one verse's translation divides the readings.
reading: Psalm 22 opens with a cry: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? Its heading in Hebrew reads "for the leader, upon *ayelet ha-shachar*," the hind of the dawn, and calls it a psalm of David. The poem moves from abandonment to a vivid description of suffering and then, in its second half, to praise and a feast for all nations. Its shape, from cry to thanksgiving, is common in the psalms.

Jewish readers have read it as David's own prayer in danger. The *Midrash Tehillim*, the midrash on Psalms, reads the hind of the dawn as Queen *Esther* and the whole psalm as her prayer before she approached the king. For that reason, some communities recite Psalm 22 on Purim. Rashi follows this line and reads the psalm as speaking for Israel in exile as well. The suffering is real, the speaker is human, and the rescue comes.

In the Gospels of Matthew and Mark, Jesus speaks the psalm's first line from the cross, in Aramaic. Christian readers from the first century on have read the whole psalm as a description of the crucifixion: the mocking, the thirst, the dividing of garments. It is read on Good Friday in many churches. As with Isaiah 53, this is Christian tradition's reading of a Jewish text, and it is described here as such.

One verse became a translation dispute. In the Hebrew Masoretic text of verse 17 (verse 16 in Christian numbering), the phrase is usually read *ka'ari*, "like a lion," at my hands and feet. The Septuagint and the Vulgate read a verb, "they pierced." The King James Version follows the Greek. JPS 1917 follows the Hebrew: "like a lion." Scholars note that the two readings differ by a single letter in Hebrew and that ancient manuscripts vary. Which text you hold decides what you can see in the verse.

words.d: "the hind of the dawn," a phrase in the heading of Psalm 22; the midrash reads it as Esther
the rabbinic midrash on the book of Psalms, which reads Psalm 22 as Esther's prayer
the queen of the book of Esther, whose prayer before approaching the king the midrash finds in Psalm 22
"like a lion," the Masoretic reading in Psalm 22:17, where the Septuagint and KJV read "they pierced"

look.title: One Letter, Two Verses
look.text: Psalm 22:16 in the King James Version (1611) reads: "For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet." The Jewish Publication Society translation (1917), numbering it 22:17, follows the Hebrew Masoretic text and gives the last phrase as "like a lion, they are at my hands and my feet." The Hebrew words differ by one letter. Ancient manuscripts and versions do not all agree.
look.prompt: Describe how a Christian reader on Good Friday and a Jewish reader on Purim would each hear this verse. Then say what a textual scholar would want to check before deciding which reading is older.

check.q: As whose prayer does the Midrash Tehillim read Psalm 22?
check.why: The midrash on Psalms reads "the hind of the dawn" as Esther and the psalm as her prayer.

check.q: What does the Hebrew Masoretic text read in Psalm 22:17 where the KJV reads "they pierced"?
check.why: The Masoretic reading is ka'ari, "like a lion," which JPS 1917 follows.

check.q: In which Gospels does Jesus speak the first line of Psalm 22 from the cross?
check.why: Matthew and Mark record the cry "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me" in Aramaic.

lessons.title: Genesis 1:26: Let Us Make
lessons.mainIdea: The plural "let us make" in Genesis 1:26 is read by the rabbis as God consulting the angels, by many church fathers as a hint of the Trinity, and by historians as a divine council or a plural of majesty.
reading: Genesis 1:26 has God say, "Let us make man in our image." The verb is plural. Every reader notices, and readers have noticed for two thousand years. The next verse switches back to the singular: God created humankind in His image. The tension between the two verses is a gap in the text, and gaps are where readings gather.

*Genesis Rabbah* (8:8) records rabbis worried that the plural would let others claim more than one God. It answers that God consulted the ministering angels before creating humans, and that the Torah kept the plural to teach humility: even the greatest should take counsel with the lesser. Rashi adopts this reading and adds that the Torah did not shy from the risk of being misread in order to teach good conduct. On this view, the plural is a lesson in manners, not a statement about God's nature.

Many early Christian writers read "let us" as a hint of the *Trinity*, the Christian teaching that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Augustine, around 400 CE, and others before him took the plural as the persons of the Godhead speaking together. This became a common Christian reading, though not all Christian scholars today hold it. It is presented here as a reading Christian tradition has offered.

Historians of the ancient Near East offer two accounts. One is the *divine council*: several biblical passages, such as 1 Kings 22:19 and Psalm 82, picture God enthroned among heavenly beings, and "let us" may address that court. The other is a *plural of majesty*, a way of speaking that some languages use for kings. Scholars debate which fits better. What they share is the question: what would this phrase have meant to its first hearers? That is a different question from the rabbis' or the church fathers', and it deserves its own answer.

words.d: the rabbinic midrash on Genesis; on 1:26 it says God consulted the angels to teach humility
the Christian teaching that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit; many church fathers read "let us" as a hint of it
the picture, in some biblical passages, of God enthroned among heavenly beings; a scholarly reading of "let us"
a way of speaking in the plural used for a king or ruler; another scholarly reading of "let us"

look.title: Three Answers to One Plural
look.text: Genesis Rabbah says God asked the angels, and the Torah kept the plural so that the great would learn to consult the small. Augustine and other church fathers say the three persons of the Trinity speak together. A historian of the ancient Near East says the phrase addresses a heavenly court, as in Psalm 82, or is the plural a king uses. Each reading explains the same word.
look.prompt: For each of the three readings, name the evidence the reader brings from outside the verse. Which readings could all be held at once by one person, and which could not?

check.q: According to Genesis Rabbah and Rashi, why does the Torah say "let us make"?
choices: Because God consulted the angels, teaching humility
Because Moses was speaking with God
Because the verb has no singular form
check.why: Genesis Rabbah 8:8 says God consulted the ministering angels, and the plural teaches the great to consult the lesser.

check.q: How did many church fathers, including Augustine, read the plural in Genesis 1:26?
choices: As a divine council of many gods
As the persons of the Trinity speaking
check.why: Many early Christian writers took "let us" as a hint of the Trinity.

check.q: Which passage do scholars cite as a picture of the divine council?
check.why: Psalm 82 and 1 Kings 22:19 picture God among heavenly beings, which supports the divine-council reading.

lessons.title: Paris 1240 and Barcelona 1263
lessons.mainIdea: Medieval disputations were staged contests in which Jewish scholars had to defend their texts before Christian judges; Ramban's account of Barcelona shows a reader arguing about what counts as binding.
reading: A *disputation* in the Middle Ages was a public debate ordered by a Christian ruler in which Jews were made to answer charges about their texts. The Jewish side could not refuse and could not win in any ordinary sense. In Paris in 1240, Nicholas Donin, a convert from Judaism, brought charges against the Talmud before the court of King Louis IX. Rabbi Yechiel of Paris and other rabbis were summoned to respond. The Talmud was condemned, and in 1242 cartloads of manuscripts were burned in Paris.

In Barcelona in 1263, the contest was over the reading of the Tanakh and the Talmud. Pablo Christiani, also a convert, argued before King James I of Aragon that rabbinic texts themselves proved that the Messiah had come. Ramban was required to answer. He later wrote his own account of the debate, and a Latin account survives from the other side. The two accounts do not agree on who prevailed. Ramban's version circulated widely among Jews; he left Aragon a few years later.

Ramban's most famous move was about categories. Christiani cited *aggadah*, rabbinic stories, as if they were binding teaching. Ramban replied that Jews are bound by the Talmud's law and by the Tanakh, but that aggadic stories are teachings a Jew may accept or set aside. Historians debate whether this was Ramban's settled view or a position for the debate. Either way, it shows a reader arguing not about a verse but about what kind of text a verse belongs to.

These events are described here as history. Jewish memory keeps them as times of pressure, and the burning of 1242 is mourned in a medieval lament still recited by some on the fast of Tisha B'Av. Christian churches today have, for the most part, renounced forced disputations. Knowing this history explains why modern dialogue between the two traditions insists on equal footing and on each side describing its own reading.

words.d: a medieval public debate, ordered by a Christian ruler, in which Jews were required to defend their texts
the rabbi who answered Nicholas Donin's charges against the Talmud in Paris in 1240
the convert who debated Ramban in Barcelona in 1263 before King James I of Aragon
rabbinic stories and non-legal teaching; Ramban argued at Barcelona that they are not binding

look.title: What Kind of Text Is This?
look.text: At Barcelona, Pablo Christiani quoted a rabbinic story that the Messiah was born on the day the Temple was destroyed. Ramban answered that he did not believe that story, and that a Jew is bound by the Tanakh and the Talmud's law, not by every aggadah. Christiani said that was evasion. Ramban said it was how Jews had always sorted their texts.
look.prompt: Is Ramban's distinction between law and story a fair rule of reading or a convenient escape? What would you need to know about how Jews used aggadah before 1263 to decide?

check.q: What happened to the Talmud after the Paris disputation of 1240?
choices: It was translated into Latin for the king
Cartloads of manuscripts were burned in 1242
It was added to the Christian canon
check.why: After the Talmud was condemned, manuscripts were burned in Paris in 1242.

check.q: Before whom did Ramban debate Pablo Christiani in 1263?
check.why: The Barcelona disputation was held before King James I of Aragon.

check.q: What was Ramban's argument about aggadah at Barcelona?
choices: That it is binding on all Jews
That it was written by Christians
That Jews may accept or set aside aggadic stories, unlike law
check.why: Ramban distinguished binding law and Tanakh from aggadic stories, which a Jew may accept or set aside.

lessons.title: Dialogue Today
lessons.mainIdea: From the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago to Nostra Aetate (1965) and Dabru Emet (2000), Jews and Christians have moved from staged contests toward voluntary dialogue.
reading: In 1893, alongside the World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago hosted the *World's Parliament of Religions*. Speakers from many faiths addressed the same hall, among them Jewish leaders such as Rabbi Emil G. Hirsch of Chicago Sinai Congregation. It was not a debate. Each speaker described his or her own tradition. Historians treat it as an early model of interfaith gathering on equal terms, though it was organized mainly by liberal Protestants and reflected that.

The Catholic Church's declaration *Nostra Aetate*, issued by the Second Vatican Council in 1965, rejected the charge that Jews as a people were responsible for the death of Jesus and called for dialogue and mutual respect. It affirmed the Church's roots in the Jewish scriptures. Many Protestant churches issued similar statements in the following decades. These are described here as what those churches said about their own teaching.

From the Jewish side, in 2000 a group of Jewish scholars published *Dabru Emet*, "Speak the Truth," a statement on how Jews might regard Christianity. It noted that Jews and Christians worship the same God and seek authority from the same book, while differing on how to read it. Not all Jewish leaders signed, and some criticized it. The point is that the response was voluntary and internal, which no disputation ever was.

In practice, dialogue today often means reading together. Jewish and Christian scholars sit with Isaiah 53 or Genesis 22 and say what each tradition has made of it. A historian may join and explain the text's setting. The rule of the room is the one Ms. Okafor set: describe, do not rank. That rule is also the rule of this course. Readers can hold different faith commitments and still agree about what Rashi said, what Augustine said and what the Hebrew word is.

words.d: the 1893 gathering in Chicago where speakers of many faiths, including Jewish leaders, described their traditions
the 1965 declaration of the Second Vatican Council on the Church's relation to non-Christian religions, including Judaism
"Speak the Truth," a 2000 statement by Jewish scholars on how Jews might regard Christianity
a voluntary exchange between traditions in which each describes its own reading; contrasted with disputation

look.title: From Contest to Conversation
look.cite: Standard dates; the Parliament ran with the Columbian Exposition in Chicago
look.prompt: Which of these events were ordered by a ruler and which were voluntary? What changed between the second row and the third?

check.q: What was the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions?
choices: A gathering in Chicago where speakers of many faiths described their traditions
A disputation ordered by the mayor of Chicago
A Catholic council held in Rome
A Jewish court that judged the Talmud
check.why: The Parliament, held with the Columbian Exposition, let speakers of many faiths, including rabbis, describe their own traditions.

check.q: What did Nostra Aetate (1965) do?
choices: Rejected blaming Jews as a people for the death of Jesus and called for dialogue
Added the Talmud to the Catholic canon
check.why: The Second Vatican Council's declaration rejected the collective charge and called for mutual respect.

check.q: What is Dabru Emet?
choices: A medieval lament for the burned Talmud
A 2000 statement by Jewish scholars on how Jews might regard Christianity
check.why: Dabru Emet, "Speak the Truth," was published by Jewish scholars in 2000.

lessons.title: Spinoza's Method
lessons.mainIdea: Spinoza's Theological-Political Treatise (1670) argued that the Bible should be studied like nature, from its text and history alone, and used Ibn Ezra's hints to ask whether Moses wrote all of the Torah.
reading: Baruch *Spinoza* was born in Amsterdam in 1632 to a family of Portuguese Jewish origin. In 1656 the leaders of the community placed him under *herem*, a ban, for opinions the surviving document does not spell out. He worked as a lens grinder and wrote philosophy. In 1670 he published, without his name, the *Theological-Political Treatise*. It was banned in the Netherlands a few years later. He died in 1677.

The treatise's central claim about reading is a method. Spinoza argued that the way to understand scripture is the way one understands nature: gather the data, in this case the language, the history of each book and the circumstances of its writing, and draw conclusions only from that. Meaning must come from the text itself, not from philosophy or from a church's or synagogue's authority. He called this interpreting scripture from scripture.

Applying the method, Spinoza reviewed passages that seemed to be written after Moses. He quoted Ibn Ezra's hints on Genesis 12:6 and Deuteronomy 1:2 and said openly what Ibn Ezra had only hinted. He proposed that Ezra the scribe, centuries after Moses, had compiled the Torah and the historical books from older writings. He read prophecy as the work of vivid imagination and miracles as events not understood, positions that both Jewish and Christian readers of his day rejected.

Historians of biblical study treat the treatise as a beginning of *critical study*: the reading of the Bible with the tools of history and language and without a prior commitment to its authority. Later scholars did not all share Spinoza's philosophy. Many religious scholars, Jewish and Christian, have used historical tools while keeping their faith. But the question he made public, who wrote these books and when, has been on the table ever since.

lessons.title: Wellhausen and the Four Sources
lessons.mainIdea: The documentary hypothesis, given its classic form by Wellhausen in 1878, proposed that the Torah was woven from four sources, J, E, D and P; Jewish scholars responded in different ways, and the theory has been revised.
reading: Julius *Wellhausen* (1844–1918) was a German Protestant scholar. In 1878 he published the book known in English as the Prolegomena to the History of Israel. It gave the classic form of the *documentary hypothesis*. Building on earlier scholars, he argued that the Torah combines four written sources. J uses the divine name and tells vivid stories; E prefers the word Elohim; D is Deuteronomy; and P, the *Priestly source*, cares for genealogies, ritual and the tabernacle.

Wellhausen's most contested claim was about order. He placed P last, after the Babylonian exile, which made the Torah's priestly law a late product rather than the foundation. He connected D with the reform of King Josiah in 622 BCE, an idea proposed by W. M. L. de Wette in 1805. The whole was an argument about history: the religion of Israel, on his account, developed from prophets to priests, and the Torah's final shape reflected the end of that process.

Jewish responses varied. Some Orthodox scholars, such as David Zvi Hoffmann in Berlin, wrote detailed rebuttals. Umberto Cassuto, at the Hebrew University, argued in 1941 that the changes in divine names follow meaning, not sources. Others in the Reform and Conservative movements accepted much of the method. Some also noted that Wellhausen's picture of a late, legalistic priesthood echoed Christian views of Judaism, and that critique has been taken seriously by later scholars of all backgrounds.

Today the four-source model is taught as a starting point, not a settled result. Many scholars now speak of layers and supplements rather than four complete documents, and dates for P are argued in both directions. What survives is the practice: reading the Torah for seams, repetitions and differences of style, and asking what they show about how the book came to be. That is the historian's question, and it sits beside, not above, the rabbis' and the church's.

lessons.title: Archaeology from Albright to Finkelstein
lessons.mainIdea: Archaeology has moved from William F. Albright's confidence that digging would confirm the biblical story to Israel Finkelstein's revised chronology, and the Tel Dan stele shows what an inscription can and cannot settle.
reading: William F. *Albright* (1891–1971), of Johns Hopkins University, shaped what came to be called biblical archaeology in the mid-twentieth century. He dug in the Land of Israel, dated pottery, and argued that the finds supported the broad outline of the biblical account of the ancestors and the conquest. His students dominated American study of the field for a generation. Albright was a Christian scholar and did not hide it, but his method was archaeological.

From the 1970s on, new excavations and surveys changed the picture. Many scholars concluded that there was no archaeological trace of a swift conquest of Canaan and that early Israel emerged within the land's highlands. Israel *Finkelstein* of Tel Aviv University proposed a *low chronology*, which moves some structures once credited to Solomon down to a later century. With Neil Asher Silberman he wrote The Bible Unearthed (2001), arguing that much of the Torah and Joshua through Kings took shape in the seventh century BCE, in Josiah's Judah.

Other archaeologists disagree, and the argument continues in journals and at dig sites. The debate is often described with the labels minimalist and maximalist, but most working scholars sit between them. What all sides use is the same evidence: pottery, walls, inscriptions, and the dating methods that fix them in time. The disputes are about how much the evidence can bear.

The *Tel Dan stele*, found in 1993 in northern Israel, shows the limits. It is an Aramaic inscription from the ninth century BCE in which a king boasts of defeating kings of Israel and of the "House of David." Most scholars read the phrase as naming David's dynasty, the first mention of David outside the Bible. It does not tell us anything about David's life or the size of his kingdom. An inscription confirms a name, a date, an enemy. The stories remain the Bible's own.

look.title: What the Stone Says
look.text: The Tel Dan stele is broken. Its surviving Aramaic lines have a king, probably of Damascus, claiming to have killed a king of Israel and a king of the House of David. Most scholars date it to the ninth century BCE, roughly a century after David's traditional dates. Before 1993 no text outside the Bible named David at all. The stone does not say what David did, how large his kingdom was, or whether the stories in Samuel are accurate.

lessons.title: Literary and Feminist Readers
lessons.mainIdea: Since the 1980s, literary critics such as Robert Alter and feminist readers such as Phyllis Trible have read the Tanakh for its artistry and for its women, asking what the text does rather than only who wrote it.
reading: In 1981 Robert *Alter*, of the University of California, published The Art of Biblical Narrative. He argued that the Bible's stories are carefully made, with repeated scenes, key words and telling silences, and that a reader should attend to that craft before cutting the text into sources. He named the *type-scene*, a scene the text repeats with variations, such as the meeting at a well in Genesis 24, Genesis 29 and Exodus 2. Meir Sternberg's The Poetics of Biblical Narrative (1985) went further into how the text controls what the reader knows.

Some of these tools have Jewish roots. The *leitwort*, a leading word repeated through a passage, was named by Martin Buber and Franz Rosenzweig in their German translation of the 1920s and 1930s. Rashi and the midrash had long noticed repeated words. What the new critics added was a way to talk about the whole story's design in the language of literature, alongside the historian's questions about its sources. Alter later translated the whole Hebrew Bible (2018) to show the craft in English.

*Feminist reading* asks what the text says about women and what its readers have done with that. Phyllis Trible's God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (1978) and Texts of Terror (1984) read stories such as Hagar's, Tamar's and Jephthah's daughter's closely and named their violence. Tikva Frymer-Kensky, who taught at the University of Chicago Divinity School, read the women of the Bible against the ancient Near East. Judith Plaskow's Standing Again at Sinai (1990) asked what a Jewish theology looks like when women are at the center. Avivah Zornberg reads the stories with midrash and psychology.

Each of these readers asks a question the earlier readers did not. Alter asks how the story is built. Trible asks whom the story hurts and who is listening. A historian asks where it came from. Rashi asks what the words mean and what the tradition heard. None of these questions replaces another. A student who can name the question each reader is asking has learned the main skill of this unit.

look.title: Four Readers at the Well
look.text: Genesis 24 sends Abraham's servant to a well, where Rebekah waters his camels. Genesis 29 brings Jacob to a well, where he rolls away the stone for Rachel. Exodus 2 brings Moses to a well, where he defends the daughters of a priest. Rashi explains each in turn. A source critic asks whether the scenes come from the same hand. Alter calls them one type-scene and asks what each variation tells about the hero. Trible asks what the women do and say, and who names them.
look.prompt: Take one of the three well scenes. Write the question each of the four readers would bring to it, and one thing each might notice that the others would not.
